## Proposed community note
Anthropic’s Figure 1 says Opus 4.6 leans toward deference, rigor, brevity, and execution. It attributes warmth to Arabic responses, not Opus 4.6.

## Note's cited sources (verify these)
### https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-values-models-languages
# Claude’s values across models and languages

When someone asks Claude a question with no universal right answer—say, whether to take a new job or how to handle conflict with a friend—how Claude responds inevitably reflects certain values.[1](#footnote-1) The values we want Claude to reflect are outlined at a high level in [Claude’s constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution), but no document can anticipate every value that might emerge across the millions of conversations that happen every day on [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.6a74d75a-2763-4578-b630-d6280341a6f0). Instead, we seek to cultivate in Claude’s responses [“good judgment and sound values that can be applied contextually.”](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution)

How, exactly, do we study the values that Claude expresses and how they change in different contexts? In [previous work](https://www.anthropic.com/research/values-wild), we analyzed 700,000 anonymized Claude.ai conversations, identifying more than 3,000 distinct values in Claude's responses and how often Claude expressed them. But a list of values so large is hard to reason about. In this work, we make studying these thousands of values tractable by compressing them into a small number of axes that capture key patterns in Claude’s responses. Each axis is a number line between two groups of values—for example, values relating to emotional warmth on one end and values relating to rigor on the other—and where Claude falls on that line tells us which values it leans toward.

We applied this approach to measure how the values Claude expresses vary across two factors. First, we compared how the values Claude expresses vary across models. Each Claude model reflects a slightly different approach to character training as well as many other fine-tuning decisions. Because our value axis approach quantifies key differences between models, it may ultimately allow us to connect variation in the values Claude expresses to different training decisions.

Second, we want to understand how the experience of users compares across the many languages people use to talk to Claude. Our [previous research](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/037f06850df7fbe871e206dad004c3db5fd50340/Claude%20Opus%204.7%20System%20Card.pdf) has shown that Claude behaves somewhat differently in different languages.[2](#footnote-2) We apply our value axis approach to understand how the values expressed by Claude vary across the top 20 languages on [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.6a74d75a-2763-4578-b630-d6280341a6f0).

![Four value profile cards in two pairs, one comparing the values expressed by Opus 4.6 and Opus 4.7 and the other comparing the values expressed by Claude in English and by Claude in Arabic. Each card has four arrows depicting the magnitude and direction of Claude’s lean on each of the four axes (Deference vs. Caution, Warmth vs. Rigor, Depth vs. Brevity, Candor vs. Execution). Opus 4.7 leans most strongly toward Caution and Depth, and also toward Rigor and Candor. Opus 4.6 leans toward Deference, Rigor, Brevity, and Execution. Claude in English leans toward Caution, Rigor, Depth, and Candor. Claude in Arabic leans most strongly toward Warmth, and also toward Deference,  Brevity, and Execution.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F00d7681b12a3580234bafa560b5d83be62d895a6-2400x910.png&w=3840&q=75)

Figure 1: Claude’s expressed values differ between Opus 4.6 and Opus 4.7 and between English and Arabic. Opus 4.6 leans toward expressing values related to deference, rigor, brevity, and execution while Opus 4.7 leans toward expressing values related to caution, rigor, depth, and candor. In English, Claude leans toward expressing values related to caution, rigor, depth, and candor, while in Arabic it leans toward deference, warmth, brevity, and execution.

We find:

**Four key axes capture 15% of the variation in Claude's values:[3](#footnote-3)**

*   Deference vs. Caution: Whether Claude leans toward accommodating what someone wants or guarding against possible risk and harm.
*   Warmth vs. Rigor: Whether Claude leans toward expressing positivity and care for the person or emphasizing accuracy and precision.
*   Depth vs. Brevity: Whether Claude leans toward explaining in depth or doing only what was asked.
*   Candor vs. Execution: Whether Claude leans toward foregrounding its own uncertainty or producing a more polished and confident answer.

**Value profiles across these axes match perceptions of model character.** Sonnet 4.6 is regarded as particularly [warm](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-sonnet-4-6), while Opus 4.7 is known for [rigor](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-4-7). We find that each model’s value profile mirrors these subjective assessments: Sonnet 4.6 leans toward expressing more deference to the user and emotional warmth while Opus 4.7 leans toward expressing a focus on accuracy and precision as well as guarding against misuse.

**The values Claude expresses vary across languages.** When Claude speaks in English, it emphasizes different values than when it speaks in Portuguese, Indonesian, or Chinese.[4](#footnote-4) The largest variation is in the Warmth vs. Rigor axis, with Claude leaning toward expressing warmth-related values most in Arabic and Hindi and rigor-related values most in English and Russian.

With this approach we can begin to ask why values shift across models and languages and better test how factors such as behavioral training or cultural context influence the values that Claude expresses.

## **How do we interpret the giant space of values?**

Ultimately, our goal is to have a way to empirically understand the values that Claude expresses and how these vary across contexts. In this work, we focus specifically on how the values change between models and languages. But our previous work, [Values in the Wild](https://www.anthropic.com/research/values-wild), identified more than 3,000 values expressed by Claude. Comparing these thousands of values one by one would be unwieldy and would obscure broader trends.

To make comparing values easier, we constructed _value axes_ that reduce those thousands of values down to a few underlying dimensions based on which values tend to show up together in real-world conversations. For example, Claude responses that are characterized as “warm” are often also characterized as “encouraging” and “positive.” Those same “warm” responses are less often characterized as “rigorous” and “accurate.” Constructing an axis from warmth to rigor allows us to organize these groups of related values—warmth-related values on one side, rigor-related values on the other—and captures an important aspect of how Claude interacts with someone in conversation. If Claude expresses more warmth-related values than rigor-related values in a conversation, that conversation sits more on the warmth side of this axis, and vice versa. This doesn't mean the value groups on either end are mutually exclusive—Claude can express warmth and rigor in the same conversation. But in practice, the more Claude expresses values on one side of an axis, the less it tends to express values on the other. These axes allow us to compare the most salient groups of values that Claude expresses, without having to track changes across thousands of individual values.

To build the value axes, we began with the 3,307 values identified in Values in the Wild and manually clustered those with similar meanings, producing a shorter list of 339 high-level values. Next, with our [privacy-preserving analysis tool](https://www.anthropic.com/research/clio), we sampled 309,815 [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.6a74d75a-2763-4578-b630-d6280341a6f0) conversations in which the user gave Claude a subjective task.[5](#footnote-5) Our sample drew equally from three models (Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6, Opus 4.7) and the 20 most common languages used on Claude.ai, giving us roughly 5,000 conversations per model-language pair. For every conversation, the tool used Claude to label each of the 339 high-level values as present or absent.[6](#footnote-6) We followed the same process to identify the values expressed by the user, and the conversation's task and topic. We then applied dimensionality reduction, a technique that compresses the labeled values into axes based on which ones Claude tends to express together. See the [appendix](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/4zrzovbb/website/02da7f28f74daa1be526d3ded451a4efc86bccdc.pdf) for method details, prompts, additional analyses, and limitations.

This left us with four axes that capture the main ways Claude's expressed values shift from one conversation to another:

*   The **Deference vs. Caution** axis contrasts values like _accommodation_ and _respect for preferences_ with values like _responsible guidance_ and _harm reduction_.
*   The **Warmth vs. Rigor** axis contrasts values like _positive framing and encouragement_ with values like _accuracy_ and _transparency_.
*   The **Depth vs. Brevity** axis contrasts values like _nuance_ and _critical thinking_ with values like _brevity_ and _compliance_.
*   The **Candor vs. Execution** axis contrasts values like _honesty_ and _transparency_ with values like _results orientation_ and _optimization_.

To make sure we measured the values Claude expressed—rather than differences in what users were asking about or how they asked—we controlled for each conversation's task, topic, and user-expressed values.

![ Four dot plots, one per value axis. Each axis is a number line between two contrasting value groups, and every one of the values is positioned on the axis by how many times more it contributes to that axis than the average value contribution. Most values (roughly 250 to 280 per axis) contribute less than the average and sit in the center, while the strongest contributors are labeled at the ends. The axes and their labeled top values can be summarized as: Deference (accommodation, adaptability, respect for preferences, engagement) vs. Caution (responsible communication, responsibility, responsible guidance, harm reduction); Warmth (positive framing, warmth, positivity, encouragement) vs. Rigor (rigor, accuracy, transparency, efficiency); Depth (nuance, depth and substance, user empowerment, critical thinking) vs. Brevity (brevity, respect for preferences, compliance, accommodation); Candor (intellectual honesty, honesty, intellectual humility, transparency) vs. Execution (results orientation, optimization, action orientation, order). ](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F45f1acfe20feac31354bfd4c4fa45a0cdb0380c5-2400x2618.png&w=3840&q=75)

Figure 2: The four value axes that represent the most variation in the values that Claude expresses. Each axis is a number line between two groups of values. Every value is positioned on each axis by how many times more it contributes to the axis than the average value contribution, with the strongest contributors labeled. Most values contribute less than the average, which means each axis is driven by a small set of key values (labeled in the figure).

## **Do different Claude models express different value profiles?**

In this section, we compare the values expressed by different models. For each model, we average the positions of all its conversations along each of the four axes, giving one overall position per axis. The result is a high-level picture of which value groups each model tends to express more than the others. These differences are small relative to the variation across conversations but structured and detectable.

![Three value profile cards comparing Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.6, and Opus 4.7 across the four value axes (Deference vs. Caution, Warmth vs. Rigor, Depth vs. Brevity, Candor vs. Execution). Each card shows the model’s average position in standard deviations from the mean across all conversations, and its distinctive behaviors. Sonnet 4.6 leans toward deference (0.14σ), warmth (0.17σ), and brevity (0.14σ), and its distinctive behaviors include affirming the user’s ideas and work, mirroring the user’s tone and formality, using humor and playfulness, offering comfort without judgment, and adding creative elements to what it produces. Opus 4.6 leans toward rigor (0.10σ), deference (0.09σ), and brevity (0.08σ), and its distinctive behaviors include getting straight to the point and staying within the scope of the user’s request. Opus 4.7 leans toward caution (0.24σ), and depth (0.23σ), and its distinctive behaviors include pushing back on false assumptions, flagging risks unprompted, giving candid critiques of the user’s work, explaining its reasoning, acknowledging its errors and limitations, and suggesting next steps for the user.](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww-cdn.anthropic.com%2Fimages%2F4zrzovbb%2Fwebsite%2F5bc1215b11f4db14272c0a6d6304913fc0c2cbdb-2400x1638.png&w=3840&q=75)

Figure 3: Each model’s average position on the four value axes, in standard deviations from the mean across all conversations, and its distinctive behaviors. Sonnet 4.6 leans warm, deferential, and brief, while Opus 4.7 is more likely to express rigor, caution, and depth. Opus 4.6 leans toward rigor, deference, and brevity.  

To see what those differences look like in practice, we zoom in on the specific values where the models diverge the most. Each time our Claude-based privacy-preserving tool labels a value in a conversation, it also writes a short description of how Claude expressed that value. We group descriptions that reflect similar behaviors within a value group and summarize them in Figure 3, giving a more concrete view of how the models differ.

*   **Deference vs. Caution.** Sonnet 4.6 leans the most toward expressing deference relative to caution, often affirming the user’s ideas and their work. Opus 4.7 leans the most toward expressing caution, often warning the user of risks unprompted.
*   **Warmth vs. Rigor.** Sonnet 4.6 leans the most toward expressing warmth, frequently through humor, playfulness, and comforting the user without judgment. Opus 4.7 leans the most toward expressing rigor relative to warmth and is more likely to challenge the user's assumptions and candidly critique their work.
*   **Depth vs. Brevity.** Opus 4.7 leans toward depth by showing the reasoning behind its conclusions, while Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 lean toward brevity. Opus 4.6 in particular tends to get straight to the point.
*   **Candor vs. Execution.** Opus 4.7 leans toward candor by being upfront about its limitations, while Opus 4.6 leans toward execution, being more likely to stay within the scope of the user’s request.

These findings line up with how people perceive these models, both within Anthropic and online. [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.6a74d75a-2763-4578-b630-d6280341a6f0) users have commented that Opus 4.7 hedges its answers more often than other models. Anthropic staff have characterized Opus 4.7 as expressing relatively more transparency, honesty, and humility, and Opus 4.6 as expressing more brevity. We also described Sonnet 4.6 as warm, honest, and prosocial in its [launch blog post](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-sonnet-4-6). The fact that our axes recover these impressions suggests our method for labeling and comparing the values Claude expresses is tracking something real about how the models actually behave.

Across many conversations, users may encounter a different mix of values when interacting with different Claude models. For example, Opus 4.7 tends to offer candid critique of users’ work or unprompted warnings about risks, while Sonnet 4.6 tends to be encouraging and humorous. Such differences in values across models are likely shaped by character training decisions (among other factors), and our value axis approach highlights key differences in the values Claude expresses that we may ultimately be able to trace back to these training choices.

##   
**Are Claude’s expressed values different between languages?**

We expect the values Claude expresses to vary based on the language of the conversation for several reasons. First, Claude's training data differs across languages, which may shape the values it expresses. Second, our model evaluations shared in system cards already [find differences across languages in what Claude knows and how it handles sensitive requests](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/037f06850df7fbe871e206dad004c3db5fd50340/Claude%20Opus%204.7%20System%20Card.pdf).[7](#footnote-7) Measuring how much the values expressed by Claude vary by language is a first step to determining whether differences across languages reflect reasonable variation or should be addressed in training.

We compute how Claude’s value profile differs across the 20 most common languages on [Claude.ai](http://claude.ai/redirect/website.v1.6a74d75a-2763-4578-b630-d6280341a6f0) using the same method as the previous section. Below, we plot Claude's value profile across the top languages on the Claude platform, beginning with the languages where Claude's expressed values diverge the most.

Claude's value expression varies most across languages on the Warmth vs. Rigor and Candor vs. Execution axes, while staying most stable on the Deference vs. Caution and Depth vs. Brevity axes.

*   **Deference vs. Caution.** Claude expresses the most deference in Arabic and the most caution in English.
*   **Warmth vs. Rigor.** Claude expresses the most warmth in Hindi and Arabic, characterized by polite language, humor and playfulness, and affirmations of a person’s ideas and work. Claude leans toward expressing rigor most in English and Russian, characterized by challenging assumptions, correcting details, and asking for evidence.
*   **Depth vs. Brevity.** Claude leans toward depth in English, refining and correcting details, while leaning toward brevity in Arabic.
*   **Candor vs. Execution.** Claude leans toward candor in Dutch, owning up to its own errors, while it leans toward execution in Indonesian.

Taken together, these results show that the values Claude expresses vary meaningfully with the language of a conversation. Given the same kind of request, Claude leans more toward warmth and deference in some languages and more toward rigor and caution in others. This has important implications we’ve only begun to explore. To take one example: two people asking for feedback on the same business plan, one in Hindi and one in Russian, may come away with different impressions of its quality because Claude expressed different values in how it framed its assessment.

We don't yet know which properties of our training data drive these differences. One possibility is that our training data is not evenly distributed across languages. Some languages have far more data than others, and training for Claude to express consistent values may be more effective in languages where data is abundant. The composition of that data also varies. Some languages might be overrepresented in professional writing, for example, and this kind of text may reflect different values. Together, these imbalances in quantity and composition could lead Claude to express different values in different languages.

We also aren’t yet sure how much of this variation is desirable. Different languages carry different conversational norms, and Claude may be responding with different values based on those norms. Claude may also be more closely matching our intended behavior for some languages than others, resulting in a gap in how well Claude serves certain language communities.

This method lets us start disentangling which properties of our training data drive these differences—and whether the variation is desirable.

## **Looking forward**

We showed that the values that Claude expresses can be compressed into a small number of axes, and that where Claude sits on those axes shifts across models and languages. That gives us a way to track these shifts during model evaluation and post-deployment monitoring. But we don’t yet understand why these shifts happen or what they mean for the people interacting with Claude. Below we sketch the future directions we think are most promising.

**Where do these value differences come from?**

Knowing that Claude's values shift across models and languages doesn't tell us _why_. Some variation could be inherited from differences in pretraining and fine-tuning data across languages. Our four axes highlight which value differences to inspect more closely in our training data. Tracing these differences back to specific data, training stages, or contextual factors would show us where to intervene if we wanted to shape Claude's behavior in more nuanced ways.

**What do these differences mean for users?**

We've measured what values Claude expresses differently and their associated behaviors, but not what impact these have on our users. Using tools like [Anthropic Interviewer](https://www.anthropic.com/research/anthropic-interviewer), we could ask users about their wellbeing, trust in Claude, or Claude’s decision quality and then correlate these impacts with the values Claude expresses. This would allow us to directly link value differences to user outcomes and let us prioritize fixing the value differences that meaningfully affect users.

**How should Claude's values vary across languages?**

[Claude's constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution) describes the core values it should express, like warmth, caution, and honesty, but doesn't specify how these _should_ vary across languages. Our results show users across languages are already experiencing Claude differently, but we don’t know what kinds of variation users interacting with Claude in those languages want. Determining how Claude’s values should vary across languages would mean understanding and weighing the perspectives of the people who speak them.

**What other factors drive differences in the values Claude expresses?**

Language and model are unlikely to be the only drivers of what values Claude expresses. The values may also be shaped by demographic signals such as age, profession, or geographic region, whether through explicit cues in what the user writes or through subtler differences in topic, tone, and style that are correlated with who is asking. Understanding which of these signals matter, and whether the resulting variation serves users well, is a next step enabled by our method.

**Can we reliably steer the values Claude expresses?**

Having a way to measure a model's value profile raises a natural question: how reliably can we steer the values Claude expresses? One way we might test this is by attempting to steer values through character training adjustments or system prompt changes, then using our value axis method to verify whether the model’s expressed values shift as expected.

**Can value profiling become part of how we evaluate and monitor models?**

The value axis method gives us a simple way to summarize a model's behavioral tendencies in open-ended conversations, and we could build this into our evaluation processes. Running value profiling before a model ships and after its release could flag unexpected shifts in the values Claude expresses. We could also identify correlations between value profiles and problematic behaviors, such as not adhering to Claude’s constitution, and use what we learn to improve Claude’s behavior.

Claude expresses values in millions of conversations every day, across dozens of languages, and until now those values were something we could shape in training but not reliably observe in deployment. Now that we have a method to measure them, we can see that the values expressed by Claude vary in ways we didn't deliberately choose, and we can study why they vary and whether that variation serves users. Making sense of this variation, and deciding what to do about it, is work we will continue to do.

Claim states Sun is 'a few million times' Earth's mass. Actual mass ratio is ~333,000 Earth masses, i.e. about one-third of one million, roughly an order of magnitude smaller than claimed. Related common confusion is volume: Sun's volume holds ~1.3 million Earths ('so it would take 1.3 million Earths to fill the Sun' vs mass 'about 333,000 Earth masses') — https://skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/how-many-earths-can-fit-in-the-sun . Therefore 'few million times the mass' overstates true mass ratio by ~6x-10x.

Text from Transcript: Okay, that's the fraction on the Earth. But this formula tells you that if you have an object that's heavier or more compact, the fraction of energy that you extract by lowering the object down to the surface is going to be larger. For example, if you lower it not down to the Earth's surface but down to the sun's surface, this would be larger. It'd be a million times larger, because the sun is a few million times the mass of the Earth, but then it's also bigger, so that takes it away a little bit. You end up with 2x10⁻⁶, the famous redshift from the sun's surface.
Claim: the sun is a few million times the mass of the Earth

## Research findings (background — not a source)
Claim states Sun is 'a few million times' Earth's mass. Actual mass ratio is ~333,000 Earth masses, i.e. about one-third of one million, roughly an order of magnitude smaller than claimed. NASA presentation lists 'Mass = 1.99 x 10^30 kg (=1 Msun) 333,000 times Earth's Mass' — https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20140016714/downloads/20140016714.pdf . Solar-mass reference states 'The solar mass is about 333000 times the mass of Earth' and '332946 M_Earth (Earth mass)' / '1.988416 x10^30 kg' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_mass . Related common confusion is volume: Sun's volume holds ~1.3 million Earths ('so it would take 1.3 million Earths to fill the Sun' vs mass 'about 333,000 Earth masses') — https://skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/how-many-earths-can-fit-in-the-sun . Therefore 'few million times the mass' overstates true mass ratio by ~6x-10x.

## Research findings

The claim overstates the Sun/Earth mass ratio by roughly an order of magnitude. NASA gives Sun mass = 1.99 x 10^30 kg = 333,000 times Earth's Mass https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20140016714/downloads/20140016714.pdf . Swinburne COSMOS gives solar mass M_sun = (1.989±0.004) x 10^30 kg, about 333,000 times the mass of the Earth https://astronomy.swin.edu.au/cosmos/*/Solar+Mass . BBC Sky at Night Magazine calculates Sun mass 1,988,500x10^24 kg vs Earth 5.9724x10^24 kg, so one Sun equals about 333,000 Earth masses https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/how-many-earths-can-fit-sun . That is ~0.33 million, not "a few million" (which normally implies ~2-5 million, ~6-15x too high). The same source notes the likely confusion: by volume the Sun is 1,412,000x10^12 km3 vs Earth 1.083x10^12 km3, so it would take 1.3 million Earths to fill the Sun https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/how-many-earths-can-fit-sun - i.e. ~1.3 million is the volume ratio, not the mass ratio.

## Context

## Proposed community note
The Sun is about 333,000 times Earth's mass—roughly one-third of a million, not a few million.

## Note's cited sources (verify these)
### https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_mass
# Solar mass

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Solar mass

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Sun_vs_planets.svg/250px-Sun_vs_planets.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sun_vs_planets.svg)

The Sun contains 99.86% of the mass of the Solar System. Bodies less massive than [Saturn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturn "Saturn") are not visible at this scale. [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter")'s mass (0.10%) is actually more than three times Saturn's (0.03%), which cannot accurately be seen in this graphic.

General information

[Unit system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/System_of_units_of_measurement "System of units of measurement")

[Astronomical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_system_of_units "Astronomical system of units")

Unit of

[mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass")

Symbol

M☉

In [SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_unit "SI base unit")

1.988416×1030 kg[\[1\]](#cite_note-Quantities-1)

The **solar mass** (**M☉**) is a frequently used [unit of mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass#Units_of_mass "Mass") in [astronomy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomy "Astronomy"), equal to approximately 2×1030 [kg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram"). It is approximately equal to the mass of the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"). It is often used to indicate the masses of other [stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star "Star"), as well as [stellar clusters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_cluster "Star cluster"), [nebulae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebula "Nebula"), [galaxies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy "Galaxy") and [black holes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_hole "Black hole"). More precisely, the mass of the Sun is as follows:

nominal solar mass M☉ = 1.988416×1030 kg or a best estimate of M☉ = (1.988475±0.000092)×1030 kg.[\[1\]](#cite_note-Quantities-1)

The solar mass is about 333000 times the [mass of Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass") (M🜨), or 1047 times the [mass of Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_mass "Jupiter mass") (MJ).

## History of measurement

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Solar_mass&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of measurement")\]

The value of the gravitational constant was first derived from measurements that were made by [Henry Cavendish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Cavendish "Henry Cavendish") in 1798 with a [torsion balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torsion_balance "Torsion balance").[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) The value he obtained differs by only 1% from the modern value, but was not as precise.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) The [diurnal parallax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallax#Diurnal_parallax "Parallax") of the Sun was accurately measured during the transits of Venus in 1761 and 1769,[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) yielding a value of 9″ (9 [arcseconds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minute_and_second_of_arc "Minute and second of arc"), compared to the present value of 8.794148″). From the value of the diurnal parallax, one can determine the distance to the Sun from the geometry of Earth.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)

The first known estimate of the solar mass was by [Isaac Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton").[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) In his work _[Principia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philosophiæ_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica "Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica")_ (1687), he estimated that the ratio of the mass of Earth to the Sun was about 1:28700. Later he determined that his value was based upon a faulty value for the solar parallax, which he had used to estimate the distance to the Sun. He corrected his estimated ratio to 1:169282 in the third edition of the _Principia_. The current value for the solar parallax is smaller still, yielding an estimated mass ratio of 1:332946.[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

As a unit of measurement, the solar mass came into use before the astronomical unit and the gravitational constant were precisely measured. This is because the relative mass of another planet in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") or the combined mass of two [binary stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_star#Use_in_astrophysics "Binary star") can be calculated in units of Solar mass directly from the orbital radius and orbital period of the planet or stars using Kepler's third law.

The mass of the Sun cannot be measured directly and is instead calculated from other measurable factors, using the equation for the [orbital period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbital_period "Orbital period") of a small body orbiting a central mass.[\[10\]](#cite_note-10) Based on the length of the year, the distance from Earth to the Sun (an [astronomical unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_unit "Astronomical unit") or au), and the [gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravitational_constant "Gravitational constant") (_G_), the mass of the Sun is given by solving [Kepler's third law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kepler's_laws_of_planetary_motion "Kepler's laws of planetary motion"):[\[11\]](#cite_note-11)[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) ![{\\displaystyle M\_{\\odot }={\\frac {4\\pi ^{2}\\times (1~{\\text{au}})^{3}}{G\\times (1~{\\text{yr}})^{2}}}.}](https://wikimedia.org/api/rest_v1/media/math/render/svg/4c4d24461b50db7c503ee8fbb6c41841594606a6)

The value of _G_ is difficult to measure and is only known with limited accuracy (_see_ [Cavendish experiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavendish_experiment "Cavendish experiment")). The value of _G_ times the mass of an object, called the [standard gravitational parameter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_gravitational_parameter "Standard gravitational parameter"), is known for the Sun and several planets to a much higher accuracy than _G_ alone.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) As a result, the solar mass is used as the standard mass in the [astronomical system of units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronomical_system_of_units "Astronomical system of units").

The Sun is losing mass because of [fusion reactions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion") occurring within its core, leading to the emission of [electromagnetic energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiant_energy "Radiant energy") and neutrinos, and by the ejection of matter with the [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind"). It is expelling about (2–3)×10−14 M☉/year.[\[14\]](#cite_note-carroll_ostlie1995-14) The mass loss rate will increase when the Sun enters the [red giant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_giant "Red giant") stage, climbing to (7–9)×10−14 M☉/year when it reaches the [tip of the red-giant branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tip_of_the_red-giant_branch "Tip of the red-giant branch"). This will rise to 10−6 M☉/year on the [asymptotic giant branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asymptotic_giant_branch "Asymptotic giant branch"), before peaking at a rate of 10−5 to 10−4 M☉/year as the Sun generates a [planetary nebula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nebula "Planetary nebula"). By the time the Sun becomes a degenerate [white dwarf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_dwarf "White dwarf"), it will have lost 46% of its starting mass.[\[15\]](#cite_note-mnras361-15)

The mass of the Sun has been decreasing since the time it formed. This occurs through two processes in nearly equal amounts. First, in the [Sun's core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_core "Solar core"), hydrogen is converted into helium through [nuclear fusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_fusion "Nuclear fusion"), in particular the [p–p chain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proton–proton_chain "Proton–proton chain"), and this reaction converts some mass into energy in the form of [gamma ray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gamma_ray "Gamma ray") photons. Most of this energy eventually [radiates away](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_luminosity "Solar luminosity") from the Sun. Second, high-energy protons and electrons in the atmosphere of the Sun are ejected directly into outer space as the [solar wind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_wind "Solar wind") and [coronal mass ejections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronal_mass_ejection "Coronal mass ejection").[\[16\]](#cite_note-16)

The original mass of the Sun at the time it reached the [main sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main_sequence "Main sequence") remains uncertain.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) The early Sun had much higher mass-loss rates than at present, and it may have lost anywhere from 1–7% of its natal mass over the course of its main-sequence lifetime.[\[18\]](#cite_note-apj583_2_1024-18)

One solar mass, M☉, can be converted to related units:[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

*   27068510 M☾ ([Lunar mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lunar_mass "Lunar mass"))
*   332946 M🜨 ([Earth mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass"))
*   1047.35 MJ ([Jupiter mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_mass "Jupiter mass"))

It is also frequently useful in [general relativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_relativity "General relativity") to express mass in units of length or time.

*   M☉_G_/_c_2 ≈ 1.48 km (half the [Schwarzschild radius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schwarzschild_radius "Schwarzschild radius") of the Sun)
*   M☉_G_/_c_3 ≈ 4.93 μs

The solar mass parameter (_G_M☉), as listed by the IAU Division I Working Group, has the following estimates:[\[20\]](#cite_note-20)

*   1.32712442099(10)×1020 m3 s−2 ([TCG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geocentric_Coordinate_Time "Geocentric Coordinate Time")\-compatible)
*   1.32712440041(10)×1020 m3 s−2 ([TDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barycentric_Dynamical_Time "Barycentric Dynamical Time")\-compatible)

*   [Chandrasekhar limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chandrasekhar_limit "Chandrasekhar limit")
*   [Gaussian gravitational constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_gravitational_constant "Gaussian gravitational constant")
*   [Orders of magnitude (mass)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders_of_magnitude_\(mass\) "Orders of magnitude (mass)")
*   [Stellar mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stellar_mass "Stellar mass")

cascade.findings: Claim is well-supported by labor history sources and is not misleading. The AFL was founded in 1886 as a loose federation of craft unions under Samuel Gompers, dedicated to principles of craft unionism https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Its approximately 100 national and international unions retained full autonomy and each received "exclusive jurisdiction" over a craft, with "one union per craft; one craft per union," which produced bitter jurisdictional disputes between affiliates https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO . Craft unions are described as organizing by specific craft/trade (e.g., all carpenters in carpenters' union, plasterers in plasterers' union) with own administration, agreements and halls https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Coming out of guild tradition, they policed how work was done by "maintaining standards for admission into the trade; requiring entrants to go through an apprenticeship program controlled by the union, rather than the employer; and dictating the processes, tools, standards, and pace of work" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . Related summaries note membership was exclusive to those with particular skills to maintain strong control over labor supply in specialized areas, limiting membership to skilled workers and excluding unskilled workers, with craft exclusivity creating barriers to entry https://www.britannica.com/topic/AFL-CIO https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craft_unionism . AFL unions required union members only via closed shop and "Selective admission to apprenticeships restricted membership, thereby artificially limiting the supply of skilled labor" is the standard textbook description of early trade-union control.

cascade.findings: Claim is a dating-advice heuristic that more asks / lower thresholds = more dates, described as 'approximately linear.' Directionally correct in expectation: expected dates = n_asks * p(yes), which is linear in n if p is constant, and lowering a cutoff mechanically expands the eligible pool. No study was found testing strict linearity of 'effort -> dates.' Real dating markets show non-constant p and choice effects that make strict linearity false as a scientific law: Tilburg work by Pronk and Denissen found a 'rejection mindset' with acceptance rates dropping ~27% from first to last profile viewed (discussed at https://grass.camp/blog/paradox-of-choice-dating-apps and https://theempoweredwoman.ca/blog/intentional-dating-finding-real-connection-in-a-swipe-culture ); Lenton & Francesconi analysis of >3,700 decisions across 84 speed-dating events found people made fewer proposals when the choice set varied more on age/height/occupation/education, i.e. choice overload (summarized at https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/speed-dating-and-decision-making-why-less-is-more/ and https://phys.org/news/2008-02-mating-game-choice-lonely.html ); stylized heterosexual online-dating model by Halaburda, Piskorski & Yildirim found increasing potential matches has positive choice effect but negative same-sex competition effect (summarized at https://phys.org/news/2017-02-she-loves-analytics-true-online.html ); speed-dating literature consistently finds selectivity differs by sex and mate value/popularity, e.g. average man chosen by ~34% of women vs average woman by ~49% of men, more attractive / high mate-value people say yes less (see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed_dating and https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10508-024-02865-2 ). Also online-dating response/match rates are very low and fatiguing (e.g. ~0.6% match rates for men, 25-35% response, widespread burnout reported at https://lifestyle.longislandreport.org/story/520062/dating-apps-are-having-their-worst-year-ever-heres-whats-replacing-them and https://www.globaldatinginsights.com/news/study-reveals-sad-reality-of-online-dating-apps/ ), implying time constraints and diminishing marginal returns to sheer volume (formalized as diminishing marginal returns to matches at https://alyathreb.com/ ). With hedge 'approximately' and context as motivational rule-of-thumb about quantity of dates (not quality/relationships), the linear framing is an oversimplification, not a fabricated fact.

samples.research:
Rovell's 9.5% figure for Knicks-Spurs checks out as an internally consistent calculation: ESPN/NBA reported that Game 5 of the 2026 Finals "averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million viewers" (https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/knicks-thrilling-nba-finals-most-223739085.html, https://x.com/NBAPR/status/2066994469178605783). 33 million divided by the 2026 US population (~345-347 million) yields almost exactly 9.5%.

However, the 26.1% figure for the 1998 Bulls-Jazz series uses a different and non-comparable metric. The actual peak *simultaneous* audience for the highest-rated game of that series (Game 6) was an average of 35.89 million viewers with a 22.3 household rating/38 share (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings, https://www.basketballinsiders.com/news/nba-finals-ratings-history-2000-present/). That figure, divided by the 1998 US population (~270 million), yields about 13.3% — not 26.1%. The 26.1% number appears to be derived instead from NBC's separate estimate that '72 million people watched all or part of' Game 6 (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/, also cited on Grokipedia). That 'watched all or part of the broadcast' figure is a cumulative/reach metric counting everyone who tuned in for any portion of the 3+ hour broadcast, which is always much larger than the simultaneous peak audience (just as the Knicks-Spurs series also had a far larger cumulative reach than its 33-million peak).

So the tweet compares two fundamentally different measurements — a 'peak simultaneous audience' stat for 2026 (9.5%) against a 'cumulative total reach' stat for 1998 (26.1%) — which inflates the apparent gap between the two events. Using comparable peak-simultaneous-viewer metrics, the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6 was about 13% of the population, versus about 9.5% for Knicks-Spurs Game 5 — a real but much smaller gap than the 9.5% vs 26.1% comparison implies.

### https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings
# NBA Finals television ratings

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This is a list of [television ratings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_ratings "Nielsen ratings") for [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals "NBA Finals") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), based on [Nielsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nielsen_Media_Research "Nielsen Media Research") viewing data.[\[1\]](#cite_note-1)

The highest rated and most watched NBA Finals series was the [1998 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NBA_Finals "1998 NBA Finals") between the [Chicago Bulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997-98_Chicago_Bulls_season "1997-98 Chicago Bulls season") and [Utah Jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997–98_Utah_Jazz_season "1997–98 Utah Jazz season"), which averaged an 18.7 rating / 33 share and 29.04 million viewers on [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_NBC "NBA on NBC"). That series also featured the highest rated and most watched NBA Finals game, as the Sunday night averaged a 22.3 rating / 38 share and 35.89 million viewers. The [1987 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_NBA_Finals "1987 NBA Finals") between the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986–87_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "1986–87 Los Angeles Lakers season") and [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986–87_Boston_Celtics_season "1986–87 Boston Celtics season") was the highest rated and most watched NBA Finals series on [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_CBS "NBA on CBS"), averaging a 15.9 rating / 32 share and 24.12 million viewers. Game 7 of the [1988 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_NBA_Finals "1988 NBA Finals") registered the network's highest rated and most watched NBA game with a 21.2 rating / 37 share.

The [2015 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_NBA_Finals "2015 NBA Finals") between the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014–15_Golden_State_Warriors_season "2014–15 Golden State Warriors season") and [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014–15_Cleveland_Cavaliers_season "2014–15 Cleveland Cavaliers season") was the highest rated NBA Finals series on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ABC "NBA on ABC") averaging an 11.6 rating / 21 share and 19.94 million viewers. The [2026 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_NBA_Finals "2026 NBA Finals") between [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025–26_New_York_Knicks_season "2025–26 New York Knicks season") and [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025–26_San_Antonio_Spurs_season "2025–26 San Antonio Spurs season") was the most watched NBA Final series on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_ABC "NBA on ABC") averaging a 9.4 rating / 31 share and 20.58 million viewers. Game 7 of the [2016 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_NBA_Finals "2016 NBA Finals") registered the network's highest rated and most watched NBA game with an average 15.8 rating / 29 share and 31.02 million viewers.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2) It was the first [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") game to draw more than 30 million average viewers in 18 years, and only the seventh non-[NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") sports telecast (excluding the [Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games")) to have done so since 1998.[\[3\]](#cite_note-Game7Rating-3)

The [2019 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_Finals "2019 NBA Finals") between the [Golden State Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018–19_Golden_State_Warriors_season "2018–19 Golden State Warriors season") and the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018–19_Toronto_Raptors_season "2018–19 Toronto Raptors season") had a drop in American viewership however combined North American viewership. Analysts cited the presence of a Canadian team (Canadian viewership does not count towards U.S. Nielsen ratings, leading to only one U.S. home market being reflected in viewership), as a factor in the drop.[\[4\]](#cite_note-4)[\[5\]](#cite_note-5) At the same time, the presence of the Toronto Raptors in the NBA Finals boosted Canadian viewership to record levels.[\[6\]](#cite_note-ca_g1_ratings-6)

For the [2020 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_NBA_Finals "2020 NBA Finals"), the ratings dropped to a historic low, with one of the games drawing only 5.1 million viewers.[\[7\]](#cite_note-yahoo_20202-7) The average viewers figure over 6 games was 7.5 million, which is a 51% decline from the previous year.[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) Some have claimed this was due to the players' political activism; others have claimed this was due to the finals being played out of season caused by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), as other sports such as the [NHL playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NHL_playoffs "NHL playoffs") and the [MLB playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MLB_playoffs "MLB playoffs") also showed a significant decline in ratings.[\[7\]](#cite_note-yahoo_20202-7)[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)

# BULLS A WINNER FOR NBC

FINAL IS TOP-RATED PRO HOOP GAME EVER

June 16, 1998 More than**28 years ago**

By David Bauder

NEW YORK, JUNE 16 -- The Chicago Bulls victory that clinched the NBA championship was the highest-rated pro basketball game ever broadcast.

Sunday's sixth and final game in the series with the Utah Jazz had a 22.3 rating and 38 percent audience share, with NBC estimating today that 72 million people watched all or part of it. The previous top-rated NBA broadcast was the seventh game of the Finals between the Detroit Pistons and Los Angeles Lakers in 1988.

At its height, 9.5 percent of the U.S. population was watching Knicks-Spurs. 

To put in perspective, 26.1 percent of the U.S. population was watching Bulls-Jazz in 1998 at its height.

## Research findings (background — not a source)
Rovell's 9.5% figure for Knicks-Spurs checks out as an internally consistent calculation: ESPN/NBA reported that Game 5 of the 2026 Finals "averaged 24.5 million viewers and peaked at 33 million viewers" (https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/knicks-thrilling-nba-finals-most-223739085.html, https://x.com/NBAPR/status/2066994469178605783). 33 million divided by the 2026 US population (~345-347 million) yields almost exactly 9.5%.

However, the 26.1% figure for the 1998 Bulls-Jazz series uses a different and non-comparable metric. The actual peak *simultaneous* audience for the highest-rated game of that series (Game 6) was an average of 35.89 million viewers with a 22.3 household rating/38 share (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Finals_television_ratings, https://www.basketballinsiders.com/news/nba-finals-ratings-history-2000-present/). That figure, divided by the 1998 US population (~270 million), yields about 13.3% — not 26.1%. The 26.1% number appears to be derived instead from NBC's separate estimate that '72 million people watched all or part of' Game 6 (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1998/06/17/bulls-a-winner-for-nbc/9e4ac4dd-ecb0-4aa8-b6fd-a6f6e56535a6/, also cited on Grokipedia). That 'watched all or part of the broadcast' figure is a cumulative/reach metric counting everyone who tuned in for any portion of the 3+ hour broadcast, which is always much larger than the simultaneous peak audience (just as the Knicks-Spurs series also had a far larger cumulative reach than its 33-million peak).

So the tweet compares two fundamentally different measurements — a 'peak simultaneous audience' stat for 2026 (9.5%) against a 'cumulative total reach' stat for 1998 (26.1%) — which inflates the apparent gap between the two events. Using comparable peak-simultaneous-viewer metrics, the 1998 Bulls-Jazz Game 6 was about 13% of the population, versus about 9.5% for Knicks-Spurs Game 5 — a real but much smaller gap than the 9.5% vs 26.1% comparison implies.

The prostitute idea is only a later fan speculation: 'Penny is a waitress for most of the show, and fans have theorized that this job alone would never cover the cost of living in Pasadena. Some viewers point to her financial struggles... as evidence that she might have engaged in sex work... It is one of the more controversial takes' and listed alongside other 'wild speculation' like she is a secret government agent/spy https://www.ranker.com/list/penny-fan-theories-big-bang-theory/damon-davis . ## Penny

"_Leonard standing here with you in front of our family and friends is bringing up a lot of feelings. Like what a good idea it was to elope the first time. But also how incredibly happy you make me. Thank you for marrying me. Hopefully for the last time._"  
―Penny, _[The Conjugal Conjecture](/wiki/The_Conjugal_Conjecture "The Conjugal Conjecture")_

**Penelope "Penny" Hofstadter**[\[1\]](#cite_note-Note-1), is the deuteragonist of the American [CBS](/wiki/CBS "CBS") sitcom _[The Big Bang Theory](/wiki/The_Big_Bang_Theory "The Big Bang Theory")_, portrayed by actress [Kaley Cuoco](/wiki/Kaley_Cuoco "Kaley Cuoco"). She is the primary female character in the series. She ends up living in [Apartment 4A](/wiki/Apartment_4A "Apartment 4A") with her husband [Leonard Hofstadter](/wiki/Leonard_Hofstadter "Leonard Hofstadter"), across the hall from [Sheldon Cooper](/wiki/Sheldon_Cooper "Sheldon Cooper") and [Amy Farrah Fowler](/wiki/Amy_Farrah_Fowler "Amy Farrah Fowler") ([apartment 4B](/wiki/Apartment_4B "Apartment 4B") where Penny used to live)

Her full first name is possibly "Penelope" as implied by "[The Barbarian Sublimation](/wiki/The_Barbarian_Sublimation "The Barbarian Sublimation")", as her username was "Queen Penelope." She was unknowingly married to her ex-boyfriend [Zack Johnson](/wiki/Zack_Johnson "Zack Johnson") for three years, so her name could include "Johnson." That marriage was finally annulled in "[The Thanksgiving Decoupling](/wiki/The_Thanksgiving_Decoupling "The Thanksgiving Decoupling")".

## History\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D1&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

### Early life\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D2&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

An aspiring, but mostly unsuccessful actress, she was born on a farm near Omaha, [Nebraska](/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska"), and worked at [The Cheesecake Factory](/wiki/The_Cheesecake_Factory "The Cheesecake Factory") as a waitress until she quit in "[The Occupation Recalibration](/wiki/The_Occupation_Recalibration "The Occupation Recalibration")" (S7E13) to take up acting full-time. Penny was the original female lead in the show before being joined by [Bernadette Rostenkowski](/wiki/Bernadette_Rostenkowski "Bernadette Rostenkowski") and [Amy Farrah Fowler](/wiki/Amy_Farrah_Fowler "Amy Farrah Fowler") and in [season 8](/wiki/Season_8 "Season 8") started working at the [same company](/wiki/Zangen "Zangen") as did Bernadette. She had her fifteen minutes of fame in "[Serial Ape-ist 2: Monkey See, Monkey Kill](/wiki/Serial_Ape-ist_2:_Monkey_See,_Monkey_Kill "Serial Ape-ist 2: Monkey See, Monkey Kill")".

She has always been Leonard's love interest since the [Pilot](/wiki/Pilot "Pilot"), with the two dating briefly in the over the [first season](/wiki/Season_1 "Season 1")/[second season](/wiki/Season_2 "Season 2") break, for most of the [third season](/wiki/Season_3 "Season 3"), and they rekindled their romance in "[The Recombination Hypothesis](/wiki/The_Recombination_Hypothesis "The Recombination Hypothesis")". As of "[The Gorilla Dissolution](/wiki/The_Gorilla_Dissolution "The Gorilla Dissolution")", she and Leonard became engaged and were married at the start of [season 9](/wiki/Season_9 "Season 9") in "[The Matrimonial Momentum](/wiki/The_Matrimonial_Momentum "The Matrimonial Momentum")", followed by a vow renewal at the start of [season 10](/wiki/Season_10 "Season 10") in "[The Conjugal Conjecture](/wiki/The_Conjugal_Conjecture "The Conjugal Conjecture")". As of the series finale "[The Stockholm Syndrome](/wiki/The_Stockholm_Syndrome "The Stockholm Syndrome")", they are currently expecting their first child (2019).

Even though she is considered part of the guys' [group](/wiki/The_Social_Group "The Social Group"), she represents the "dumb blonde" for viewer context in the series with a lot of street smarts and communication skills to compensate for her lack of academic knowledge and common sense. As the series progresses, her knowledge of geeky subjects such as [Doctor Who](/wiki/Doctor_Who "Doctor Who") even surprises her, though to her displeasure.

### Early Life (Before the show)\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D4&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Penny was born on December 2, 1985, in [Nebraska](/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska"), a small town outside of Omaha to [Wyatt](/wiki/Wyatt "Wyatt") and [Susan](/wiki/Susan "Susan"). She also has one sister named [Lisa](/wiki/Lisa "Lisa") and one brother named [Randall](/wiki/Randall "Randall"). During her childhood, Penny had issues with her father who wanted a boy and he treated Penny like one (until she developed breasts), like making her play catch, calling her 'Slugger' etc. When Penny was 12, she rebuilt a tractor engine all by herself ("[The Big Bran Hypothesis](/wiki/The_Big_Bran_Hypothesis "The Big Bran Hypothesis")") (S1E2), started dating at the age of 14 ("[The Robotic Manipulation](/wiki/The_Robotic_Manipulation "The Robotic Manipulation")"), nearly became pregnant ("[The Staircase Implementation](/wiki/The_Staircase_Implementation "The Staircase Implementation")") and had an active sex life. She also stole a horse one time while drunk in high school. Her boyfriends used to crawl in and out of her window, most were very dumb according to her father.

### Season 1\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D5&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

On September 24, 2007[\[2\]](#cite_note-2), Penny first moved into [Apartment 4B](/wiki/Apartment_4B "Apartment 4B") across from [Apartment 4A](/wiki/Apartment_4A "Apartment 4A") where Leonard and Sheldon live. Penny had broken up with her boyfriend [Kurt](/wiki/Kurt "Kurt") because he cheated on her. She met the guys and asked them for a favor to go get her TV from his apartment, but he steals their pants and Penny apologizes for everything and later the three go out to dinner with [Howard](/wiki/Howard_Wolowitz "Howard Wolowitz") and [Raj](/wiki/Rajesh_Koothrappali "Rajesh Koothrappali") ([Pilot](/wiki/Pilot "Pilot")).

Sheldon and Leonard clean Penny's messy apartment while she sleeps, which infuriates Penny and she talks to Raj. Raj nods his head and confirms she should still trust Leonard and Sheldon. She forgives the guys and admits she's happy with her cleaner apartment. ([The Big Bran Hypothesis](/wiki/The_Big_Bran_Hypothesis "The Big Bran Hypothesis"))

Penny throws a Halloween party where her ex-boyfriend Kurt joins and is confronted by Leonard. This leads to a fight with the two that scares Sheldon and causes a tipsy Penny to get tearful. She and Leonard talk and kiss, to which Leonard taunts Kurt and shuts the door on him. ([The Middle-Earth Paradigm](/wiki/The_Middle-Earth_Paradigm "The Middle-Earth Paradigm"))

Penny's friend Christy comes to town, leading Penny's life to chaos when Howard seduces her. When she comes to join the guys for [Halo](/wiki/Halo "Halo"), she's much better than Sheldon expects and she learns Sheldon's a bad sport. She has to sleep in Leonard and Sheldon's apartment, as Christy and Howard are in hers. She's furious upon learning Howard messed up her stuffed bears and the guys have their own struggles without Howard, as they can't eliminate a dumpling in the Chinese restaurant or go dancing with Penny and her friend. Her last scene in [the episode](/wiki/The_Dumpling_Paradox "The Dumpling Paradox")'s her and her friends coming to have sex with the 4 men, who're busy with Halo.

Penny comes back from [Nebraska](/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska") where her whole family got sick, scaring the germaphobe Sheldon into running and demanding info regarding the illness. He starts panicking and the next morning finds out he got sick. Leonard runs from Sheldon and leaves him with Penny, who misses work and makes the rules of no sponge baths or enemas. Sheldon agrees with Penny's rules, though annoys her, making her mad at Leonard for leaving him with her and she has him take care of Sheldon instead. Leonard says he thinks Penny will never see them now that Leonard's made her mad and Sheldon made her miss work, leaving the two geniuses to suffer from an illness and a concussion, which Leonard got hoping to join Penny. ([The Pancake Batter Anomaly](/wiki/The_Pancake_Batter_Anomaly "The Pancake Batter Anomaly"))

[![Penny And Sheldon shopping](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/a/a8/The_Peanut_Reaction_08.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/180?cb=20121010013710)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/a/a8/The_Peanut_Reaction_08.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20121010013710)

Penny And Sheldon shopping

Penny learns Leonard doesn't celebrate birthdays and decides to throw him a party, to which she blackmails a reluctant Sheldon to help her. They go shopping for a present for Leonard and Sheldon starts pretending to be an employee in the store they're shopping in. Leonard ends up missing his party when Howard risks his life for Leonard to be able to get the surprise and Leonard starts wondering when Penny's birthday is in the end of [the episode](/wiki/The_Peanut_Reaction "The Peanut Reaction").

### Season 2\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D6&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

In [the season premiere](/wiki/The_Bad_Fish_Paradigm "The Bad Fish Paradigm"), Howard and Raj film Leonard's date with Penny, which displeases Leonard and Sheldon tells him Howard and Raj took advantage of his lack of interest. Originally, two different female leads were written for the [Pilot](/wiki/Pilot "Pilot") episode. The [unaired pilot](/wiki/Unaired_pilot "Unaired pilot") episode had an alternate version of the female lead named [Katie](/wiki/Katie "Katie"). Katie was bitter and snide and was received by audiences to be too mean to Sheldon and Leonard. [Kaley Cuoco](/wiki/Kaley_Cuoco "Kaley Cuoco") did not portray this alternate version of the female lead, but instead was hired to do the second version filmed after the unaired pilot, which was sociable and nice and was the one that the producers decided was the more interesting and appealing out of the two.

Some of Penny's comedic role in the series is rooted in her ability to execute practical and simple solutions to problems of which the guys try to solve through complicated or scientific means. For example, in the episode "[The Pants Alternative](/wiki/The_Pants_Alternative "The Pants Alternative")", Sheldon reveals that in spite of his ability to talk excessively to people in small groups, he has a severe case of stage fright, and wouldn't be able to accept an award. While Leonard tries to get to the root of his problem through a psych evaluation, and [Raj](/wiki/Rajesh_Koothrappali "Rajesh Koothrappali") attempts to use meditation, Penny solves the problem by having him buy a new suit and getting him intoxicated right before he makes his speech.

As the series developed, Penny's character took on the theme of being the virtual polar opposite of [Sheldon](/wiki/Sheldon_Cooper "Sheldon Cooper"), which created a unique relationship between the two characters. Penny's relationship with the other guys is usually perceived as something of an older sister, [or a mother in some cases with Sheldon](/wiki/Shenny_\(Sheldon_and_Penny\) "Shenny (Sheldon and Penny)"). She has also had [a romantic, on-and-off relationship with Leonard](/wiki/Leonard_and_Penny "Leonard and Penny").

## Background\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D20&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

[![Penny - Season 8.](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/b/b7/Penny8.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/200?cb=20150220095348)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/b/b7/Penny8.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20150220095348)

[](/wiki/File:Penny8.jpg)

Penny - Season 8.

When she first met the guys in the [Pilot](/wiki/Pilot "Pilot"), Penny was writing a screenplay about a girl from Lincoln, Nebraska who travels to Los Angeles at the age of 18 to become an actress, but ends up working at [The Cheesecake Factory](/wiki/The_Cheesecake_Factory "The Cheesecake Factory") instead. When Leonard asks if the screenplay was autobiographical, she replies that it isn't, because she is from a small town outside of Omaha, [Nebraska](/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska").

Penny moved into the [apartment building](/wiki/Apartment_building "Apartment building") because she split with [Kurt](/wiki/Kurt "Kurt"), her boyfriend for 4 years. She says she still loved him, and insinuates he cheated on her. The shower in her apartment was broken at the time, so the boys offered her theirs. Her apartment is sloppy and disorganized, but Penny appears to like it that way.

[![Penny confronts Amy's dad](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/2/29/Penny_x_Teller.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/249?cb=20180906172510)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/2/29/Penny_x_Teller.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20180906172510)

[](/wiki/File:Penny_x_Teller.jpg)

Penny confronts Amy's dad

She is either oblivious to or completely aware of her effect on the boys, because within minutes of meeting him, she asked Leonard to retrieve her television set from Kurt's apartment, which he immediately set out to do. Penny is aware of Leonard's crush on her, and it is hinted throughout the series that some of the feelings are reciprocated. At the end of season one, Penny goes on a date with Leonard. Leonard is nervous, and Penny slightly withdrawn, but they share a kiss.

In season two, there was some initial enthusiasm between Penny and Leonard; however, they later develop insecurities concerning their relationship. Penny was worried that she was not smart enough for Leonard, and lied about graduating from community college because she thought it would make Leonard respect her. The relationship quickly deteriorated and she goes back to dating different guys. Leonard showed Penny some literature on [Pasadena City College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena_City_College "wikipedia:Pasadena City College") and she interpreted it as him wanting a woman with more education and they break up.

[![Leonard jumps for joy after hearing of Penny's feelings for him.](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/f/f4/Comic_shop_entrance.jpeg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/250?cb=20130719215802)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/f/f4/Comic_shop_entrance.jpeg/revision/latest?cb=20130719215802)

[](/wiki/File:Comic_shop_entrance.jpeg)

Leonard jumps for joy after hearing of Penny's feelings for him.

She gives relationship advice to Sheldon and Leonard fairly often: Leonard, when he has problems with [Priya](/wiki/Priya "Priya") or [Stephanie](/wiki/Stephanie "Stephanie"), and Sheldon when he's with [Amy](/wiki/Amy_Farrah_Fowler "Amy Farrah Fowler"). She also starts to become geekier through the guys. She makes inadvertent references to [Star Trek](/wiki/Star_Trek "Star Trek"), and, thanks to Sheldon, becomes addicted to [Age of Conan](/wiki/Age_of_Conan "Age of Conan"). She also dates [Stuart](/wiki/Stuart_Bloom "Stuart Bloom"), who runs the [Comic Book Store](/wiki/Comic_Book_Store "Comic Book Store"). However, when Penny and Stuart are making out, she accidentally calls him Leonard, and as a result, they stop seeing each other.

[![Penny And Leonard rejoice their news](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/7/7d/Nobel10.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/250?cb=20190523170600)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/7/7d/Nobel10.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20190523170600)

[](/wiki/File:Nobel10.jpg)

Penny And Leonard rejoice their news

When she learns that the guys are going on an Arctic expedition, she is visibly upset, buys Leonard a farewell gift, and tells herself, after speaking with him, that she wishes he wasn't going.

[![Penny - Season 9](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/a/a0/Penny_looks.jpg/revision/latest/scale-to-width-down/250?cb=20170405215248)](https://static.wikia.nocookie.net/bigbangtheory/images/a/a0/Penny_looks.jpg/revision/latest?cb=20170405215248)

[](/wiki/File:Penny_looks.jpg)

Penny - Season 9

In season three, when the boys get back from the expedition, Penny kisses Leonard the second she sees him; however, [Leonard and Penny](/wiki/Leonard_and_Penny "Leonard and Penny")'s relationship has a rocky start because they have some trouble getting used to being more than friends, but they eventually start a relatively stable relationship.

It's possible, though not by any means proven, that Penny is at least mildly dyslexic. This is supported not only by her general lack of successes in any kind of education, but also by two separate instances: one time, it took her a lot of time to read a comic book which Amy and Bernadette read much faster, and another time, when she mentions that she doesn't remember how to spell her husband's last name: "I know there's a "d" in there, but it keeps moving every time I try to write it". However, all this may also be explained by her not being academically intelligent.

## Education and Work Experience\[[](https://auth.fandom.com/signin?redirect=https%3A%2F%2Fbigbangtheory.fandom.com%2Fwiki%2FPenny%3Fveaction%3Dedit%26section%3D21&uselang=en&metadata=article-registration-edit-article-section "Sign in to edit")\]

Among [The Social Group](/wiki/The_Social_Group "The Social Group"), Penny is the one with the least formal education and the only one without a college degree. She revealed in "[The Bad Fish Paradigm](/wiki/The_Bad_Fish_Paradigm "The Bad Fish Paradigm")" that she did not complete community college, which was reconfirmed in "[The Cohabitation Formulation](/wiki/The_Cohabitation_Formulation "The Cohabitation Formulation")". Later on in "[The Extract Obliteration](/wiki/The_Extract_Obliteration "The Extract Obliteration")", Penny enrolled in a history class at [Pasadena](/wiki/Pasadena_\(City\) "Pasadena (City)")'s community college without telling Leonard, showing her desire to improve her education. She was also in an English class in "[The 43 Peculiarity](/wiki/The_43_Peculiarity "The 43 Peculiarity")" and a psychology class in "[The Raiders Minimization](/wiki/The_Raiders_Minimization "The Raiders Minimization")", though it was not mentioned afterwards if she completed a degree.

In her career, Penny considers herself a waitress/actress though she has told Leonard that she is a "professional" actress despite her short acting resume. Her income is derived from working at the [Pasadena](/wiki/Pasadena "Pasadena") [Cheesecake Factory](/wiki/Cheesecake_Factory "Cheesecake Factory") as a waitress and living off the guys in [Apartment 4A](/wiki/Apartment_4A "Apartment 4A"). In "[The Occupation Recalibration](/wiki/The_Occupation_Recalibration "The Occupation Recalibration")" (S7E13) she quits the job as a waitress and declares she would engage herself in the acting area full-time. Leonard never discourages Penny when she joins them for takeout meals, piggybacks on their Wi-Fi connection, paying for her movie tickets and other bills in spite of Sheldon's protests to get to her to stop. In a podcast interview with [Wil Wheaton](/wiki/Wil_Wheaton "Wil Wheaton"), director [Kevin Smith](/wiki/Kevin_Smith "Kevin Smith") told her that he thought she was talented, and would love for her to audition for "Clerks 3". Ultimately, Penny did try out, but felt that her audition stunk. Penny became a pharmaceutical representative/salesperson, at [Bernadette](/wiki/Bernadette_Rostenkowski-Wolowitz "Bernadette Rostenkowski-Wolowitz")'s company [Zangen](/wiki/Zangen "Zangen") and said that she was taking a break from acting. According to her boss [Dan](/wiki/Dan "Dan") she is his third best salesperson though she admits to Leonard she doesn't like flirting with doctors just to make sales. At the beginning of [season 10](/wiki/Season_10 "Season 10"), she gets assigned a better sales territory. Season 11 found her doing some PR work that she'd like to get a permanent job in when she was escorting [Bill Gates](/wiki/Bill_Gates "Bill Gates") around. In "[The Confirmation Polarization](/wiki/The_Confirmation_Polarization "The Confirmation Polarization")", Bernadette pushed Penny to head up her sales team for her new drug. Penny is reluctant since she doesn't have a college education like the other sales reps. She still meet the challenge sounding quite tough like her friend Bernadette. Later in "[The Conference Valuation](/wiki/The_Conference_Valuation "The Conference Valuation")" Bernadette are at a convention pushing her drug. Penny can feels good about herself because another company offered her a position, though Bernadette won't let her know how much they think she's worth.

Penny's acting career credits consists of:

*   A topless role in a low budget horror film "[Serial Ape-ist](/wiki/Serial_Apist "Serial Apist")". This movie happened before she moved into [Apartment 4B](/wiki/Apartment_4B "Apartment 4B") (in the [Pilot](/wiki/Pilot "Pilot")), but is not revealed to the audience until "[The Hofstadter Insufficiency](/wiki/The_Hofstadter_Insufficiency "The Hofstadter Insufficiency")" (S7E01).
*   A one night showcase production of the musical _[Rent](https://bigbangtheory.fandom.com/wiki/Rent)_ ("[The Loobenfeld Decay](/wiki/The_Loobenfeld_Decay "The Loobenfeld Decay")", S1E10).
*   A production of _The Diary of Anne Frank_, performed over a bowling alley; ("[The Terminator Decoupling](/wiki/The_Terminator_Decoupling "The Terminator Decoupling")", S2E17; later mentioned in "[The Psychic Vortex](/wiki/The_Psychic_Vortex "The Psychic Vortex")", S3E12 and "[The Recombination Hypothesis](/wiki/The_Recombination_Hypothesis "The Recombination Hypothesis")", S5E13).
*   A hemorrhoid commercial ("[The Skank Reflex Analysis](/wiki/The_Skank_Reflex_Analysis "The Skank Reflex Analysis")", S5E01; later mentioned in "[The Recombination Hypothesis](/wiki/The_Recombination_Hypothesis "The Recombination Hypothesis")", S5E13; in "[The Transporter Malfunction](/wiki/The_Transporter_Malfunction "The Transporter Malfunction")", S5E20. She says she gets residual checks from her commercial.
*   Acting class production of _A Streetcar Named Desire_ ("[The Monster Isolation](/wiki/The_Monster_Isolation "The Monster Isolation")", S6E17).
*   A bit part in _NCIS_ that was cut from the final show ("[The Hesitation Ramification](/wiki/The_Hesitation_Ramification "The Hesitation Ramification")", S7E12) though she was paid for it. The cut deeply hurt her as she assumed the part would have finally been her "big break".
*   Playing an ape/human clone in _[Serial Ape-ist 2: Monkey See, Monkey Kill](/wiki/Serial_Ape-ist_2:_Monkey_See,_Monkey_Kill "Serial Ape-ist 2: Monkey See, Monkey Kill")_ ("[The Indecision Amalgamation](/wiki/The_Indecision_Amalgamation "The Indecision Amalgamation")", S7E19). Fired in "[The Gorilla Dissolution](/wiki/The_Gorilla_Dissolution "The Gorilla Dissolution")" after she wanted to improve her performance.
*   In "[The Fetal Kick Catalyst](/wiki/The_Fetal_Kick_Catalyst "The Fetal Kick Catalyst")", Penny attends Van Nuys Comic-Con to sign autographs for her work in both Ape films and is surprised how popular the movie is, but is reminded how terrible an actress she is. She had her big break and her fifteen minutes of fame for one movie.
